newsitem.title: GERMANY: German SPD raps Kohl on Bonn-Paris ties.
newsitem.headline: German SPD raps Kohl on Bonn-Paris ties.

text.p: Germany's opposition Social Democrats said on Tuesday the Bonn-Paris axis at the heart of European integration was under strain and accused Chancellor Helmut Kohl of toning down his commitment to the cause.

Party chairman Oskar Lafontaine and parliamentary leader Rudolf Scharping told a news conference to review the first half of Germany's four-year parliamentary term that Germany was not on France's wavelength, particularly on unemployment.
"The entire French elite believes Germany's financial policies are wrong," Lafontaine said.

Scharping said the link between Bonn and Paris was "under more strain than the German public believes", warning this could have serious implications for plans to reform the Maastricht Treaty on European Union.
"A reform of the Maastricht treaty is only possible in the long term when the Franco-German axis is working and that is sadly not as I would wish," he said.
Scharping said recent comments by Kohl had raised questions about the veteran chancellor's commitment to a cause he has driven forward like few other post-war politicians.
He called on Kohl to speak to parliament before a summit of European leaders in Dublin in December and state his determination to press on along the path towards integration.

"I hope very much...the chancellor will make clear his commitment to European integration, which has been somewhat reduced at present, and that any ambiguous statements can be put to one side," Scharping said.
Officials from the EU's 15 member states and the European Commission are negotiating to create a reformed Maastricht treaty, sometimes known as "Maastricht II".

Some commentators in the German press interpreted remarks by Kohl on a trip to Dublin earlier this month about the possibility of a "Maastricht III" treaty as an admission by the ardent European the current reform would not go far enough.

Kohl worked closely with Francois Mitterrand during the French socialist's two presidential terms. Since the election of Jacques Chirac last year, both countries have been at pains to stress that their bilateral ties remain excellent.

Lafontaine also took a swipe at Germany's independent central bank, the Bundesbank, saying it was pursuing an ultra-cautious interest rate policy instead of encouraging more economic growth to try to cut unemployment across Europe.
He said Europe was being punished by inflexible policies at the centre of the continent's biggest economy.
"I fail to understand why the German government sticks by its failed economic and finance policies while the whole of Europe has to pay for it through more and more job losses."

He cited an article in the German business daily Handelsblatt by former French Prime Minister Edouard Balladur calling for the Bundesbank make more use of its room for manoeuvre in interest-rate policy.
Scharping praised a speech by Chirac to the International Labour Organisation in June on ways to fight unemployment.
"It was totally different from what the chancellor said on his compulsory visit to (the Federal Labour Office in) Nuremberg this summer," he said.
